verdicts.trueWording: Beads on a string: stories plus interlinking interstitial narrative
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. Page verbatim: 'So we begin with two books of stories with an interlinking interstitial narrative, which we sometimes call the beads on a string. Where each story is a bead and the interstitial is the string that ties them all together. There are two volumes of that, with the third being the true mosaic novel.' Speaker is Martin in the SFFWorld interview reprinted at WildCardsWorld; the two non-mosaic volumes of the triad are exactly what he is describing. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Dramatic/salacious sections last a few pages, then brisk summary
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. PW review of Fire & Blood (Bantam, ISBN 978-1-5247-9628-0, reviewed 11/19/2018) reads verbatim: 'Brief sections are dramatic (“the golden dragon devoured the queen in six bites”) or salacious (“it aroused the princess to watch the men disporting with one another”), and there are entertaining snatches of dialogue and detailed depictions of battles, but they only last a few pages before a return to brisk summary.' Quote exact; publication and book both correct.

verdicts.trueWording: Different prose style from the novels; dry, staid, objective tone
verdicts.note: Live tor.com returned HTTP 403; recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20200116004102id_/https://www.tor.com/2018/11/21/grrm-fire-and-blood-review/ (raw HTML, not a summarizer). Byline 'Chris Lough', Wed Nov 21 2018. Verbatim: 'Fire & Blood is also written in a different style of prose than the primary Song of Ice and Fire novels; featuring a dry, staid, objective tone...'. Both limbs (the tone, and the contrast with the ASOIAF novels) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Not a novel; an entirely different form from popular history
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. 'Imaginary History: PW Talks With George R.R. Martin', by Lenny Picker, Jul 16 2018. Martin verbatim: 'The important thing, as I keep stressing, is that it’s not a novel... they’re getting the latest Ice and Fire novel, which is an entirely different literary form than what’s essentially a popular history.' Quote exact. Note the page phrases the contrast the other way round (the novel is the different form from the popular history), but the claim's substance — F&B is not a novel, it is essentially a popular history, a different literary form — is fully carried.

verdicts.trueWording: Co-writers pored over 10,000 pages, pulling out all such references
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. BookPage, 'George R.R. Martin: History is written in blood', interview by Cat Acree, December 2014. Verbatim: 'Elio M. García and Linda Antonsson, founders of the fan site Westeros.org... As co-writers, they pored over 10,000 pages of novels, pulling out all references to history, myths and legends.' Every limb supported; the book is The World of Ice and Fire.

verdicts.trueWording: A Game of Thrones scores between 4 and 4.5, quite low
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. A.R. Rivera, 'A Brief Linguistic Exam of ‘A Song Of Ice And Fire’', 09/10/2023. Verbatim in the lexical-density paragraph: 'A Game of Thrones has a score between 4 and 4.5, which is quite low, compared to the first Harry Potter book...'. The preceding sentence establishes the metric is lexical density, so the claim's 'lexical density score' limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: ARI score for A Game of Thrones is sixth-grade, 11-12 years old
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. Same Rivera post. Verbatim: 'The readability factor is determined by the Automated Readability Index (ARI)... The ARI score for A Game of Thrones is sixth-grade, or 11-12 years old (medium.com).' The page itself sources the figure to medium.com, but the claim only asserts that this reading gives that score, which it does.

verdicts.trueWording: First four ASOIAF books rendered searchable in their entirety
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. Nine Worlds Academia 2014 abstract, 'Writing Westeros: a Corpus Linguistic Study of A Song of Ice and Fire', Matthew Voice, University of Sheffield. Verbatim: 'With the aid of contemporary software, the first four books of ASOIAF are rendered searchable in their entirety, and quantifiable patterns of language can be extracted.' The stylistic-analysis limb is carried by 'Breaking down the means of stylistic analysis and characterisation' later in the same abstract.

verdicts.trueWording: One source of tension and ~20 main characters in five chapters
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. Fiction Advocate, 'How to Write Like George R. R. Martin', Jan 28 2015, signed 'Graham Oliver is a graduate student in Austin, Texas.' Verbatim in section 1 ('Keep it simple. Then build.'): 'Martin has introduced a source of tension (Others) and 20 or so main characters within the first five chapters.' The A Game of Thrones limb is explicit two sentences earlier. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Pairing exposition with the dramatic reduces losing the reader
verdicts.note: Live fetch, 200. Same Graham Oliver piece, end of section 1. Verbatim: 'By pairing the exposition with the dramatic, you reduce the chances of losing the reader.' The 'without stalling the reader' limb is supported by the immediately preceding sentence: 'the plot points allow for exposition to happen seamlessly, without losing the reader’s interest.'

verdicts.trueWording: 0.46% ly-adverbs, 3rd percentile of all books in our library
verdicts.note: prosecraft.io is defunct (curl returned exit 0 bytes / no connection). Recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20181027143335id_/http://prosecraft.io/library/george-r-r-martin/a-knight-of-the-seven-kingdoms/ — a 2018 capture, matching the citation. Metrics block reads: '0.46% ly-adverbs / 3rd PERCENTILE of all the books in our library'. Book page is A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms by George R. R. Martin, 104,449 total words, 'this is a SHAXPIR project'. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 2.26% all adverbs, 9th percentile of all books in our library
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture (20181027143335). Metrics block reads: '2.26% all adverbs / 9th PERCENTILE of all the books in our library'. Both the percentage and the percentile limbs are exact.

Same Wayback raw capture. Metrics block reads: '1.80% non-ly-adverbs / 34th PERCENTILE of all the books in our library', and separately '0.46% ly-adverbs / 3rd PERCENTILE'. The comparative limb ('far higher than the same book’s 3rd-percentile ly-adverb rank') is a direct arithmetic reading of two figures both present on the same page, so it is supported rather than inferred from outside.

verdicts.trueWording: 7.74% passive voice, 43rd percentile of all books in our library
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Metrics block reads: '7.74% passive voice / 43rd PERCENTILE of all the books in our library'. Both limbs exact.

verdicts.trueWording: Analyzed hundreds of millions of words from thousands of authors
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture, in the 'clippings from this book' block: 'We’ve analyzed hundreds of millions of words, from thousands of different authors, training our linguistic models to recognize the most vivid words in the English language… the words that create the most intense sensory experiences: colors, textures, sounds, flavors, and aromas.' The 'vividness model' limb is supported — the same sentence names vividness as what the models are trained to recognize, and the page reports a 62.82% vividness metric.
